uncited: Illumination and Tone Shading Models provide non-photorealistic lighting cues to enhance the visual clarity and artistic style of volume renderings.

Unlike photometric models that simulate physical light transport, these methods map geometric or scalar properties to pre-defined color variations, prioritizing interpretability and aesthetic control over physical accuracy.

They are distinct from [Geometric Buffers](781-geometric-buffers-g-buffers.md) by focusing on color modulation rather than depth/normal encoding, and from [Base Gaseous Illumination Renderer](794-base-gaseous-illumination-renderer.md) by incorporating directed shading components.
The family shares the goal of enhancing volume visualization through stylized lighting.
All methods operate on fragment-level data, typically utilizing the volume sample gradient as a proxy for surface normal orientation.
They decouple illumination from the physical light transport equation, instead using mathematical functions of the view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color.
Common inputs include the normalized gradient $\nabla f_n$, light vectors $L$, and base colors derived from transfer functions.
The output is a final color $c$ that combines ambient/gaseous components with directed illumination effects.
The concept of non-photorealistic volume rendering emerged to address the ambiguity of standard volume rendering, where internal structures can be hard to distinguish.
Early work focused on enhancing edge detection and silhouette rendering.

The specific illumination models in this family, such as Lit Sphere Shading and Volume Illustration Tone Shading, were developed to provide intuitive lighting cues that help viewers perceive shape and depth in volumetric data without the computational cost of full global illumination.
These techniques are widely used in medical visualization, scientific data exploration, and artistic volume rendering.
